titulo: Sounds, alphabet and first words: Vowels, double consonants and stress

aula.objetivo: Read the Italian alphabet aloud, pronounce the vowels purely, apply the soft and hard rules of «c», «g» and «sc», hear double consonants and stress, and greet people with the right form for a friend and for a stranger.

blocos.contexto: Paolo runs a café. Signora Rossi and her friend Luca drop by. Listen for the two ways of asking «How are you?»: «Come sta?» and «Come stai?».

linhas.pt: — Good morning, Mrs Rossi! How are you?

linhas.ru: — Buongiorno, Paolo! Sto bene, grazie. E Lei?
linhas.pt: — Good morning, Paolo! I'm fine, thank you. And you?
linhas.audio: Buongiorno, Paolo! Sto bene, grazie. E Lei?

linhas.pt: — Fine, thank you. Here's your coffee.

linhas.ru: — Grazie mille! Ah, ecco Luca! Ciao, Luca! Come stai?
linhas.pt: — Thanks a lot! Ah, here is Luca! Hi, Luca! How are you?
linhas.audio: Grazie mille! Ah, ecco Luca! Ciao, Luca! Come stai?

linhas.ru: — Buongiorno, signora! Sto bene, grazie. E Lei?
linhas.pt: — Good morning, madam! I'm fine, thank you. And you?
linhas.audio: Buongiorno, signora! Sto bene, grazie. E Lei?

linhas.ru: — Bene, bene. Paolo, un cappuccino per Luca, per favore?
linhas.pt: — Fine, fine. Paolo, a cappuccino for Luca, please?
linhas.audio: Bene, bene. Paolo, un cappuccino per Luca, per favore?

linhas.pt: — Right away! Here you are, Luca.

blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: English vowels often glide into a second sound: «go» becomes «goh-oo», «day» becomes «deh-ee». Italian vowels do not. Say each one cleanly and hold it still. STEP 2: «a» is always «ah». «E» is «eh» as in «bed». «I» is «ee» as in «machine». «O» is «oh» as in «more». «U» is «oo» as in «food». STEP 3: the final vowel is always pronounced. «Bene» is not «been»: it is «BEH-neh», with two clear «eh» sounds. STEP 4: do not reduce unstressed vowels. English turns the last «a» of «pasta» into «uh», but Italian keeps «ah»: «PAH-stah». STEP 5: two vowels next to each other are usually pronounced separately, one after the other. «Paolo» is «PAH-oh-loh».
blocos.comparacao: The biggest change for an English speaker is the unstressed vowel. English turns them into a quiet «uh» (the «a» in «banana»). In Italian every vowel is full, whether it is stressed or not. Practice by saying the words slowly and keeping the last vowel strong: «bene», «latte», «otto».

erros.motivo: The final «e» is pronounced «eh», it is not silent.
The word ends in «e», and it is pronounced.

blocos.titulo: Double consonants and where the stress falls
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: a doubled letter is pronounced longer, almost as if you hold the consonant for a beat before you release it. «Palla» (ball) is not «pala» (shovel). «Nonno» (grandfather) is not «nono» (ninth). STEP 2: English does not do this inside a word, but you can feel it if you say «book case» or «night time» slowly: the sound is held between the two words. Italian does it inside one word: «sette» is SEHT-teh, with a short pause on the «t». STEP 3: most Italian words are stressed on the second-to-last syllable: «ca-FFÈ» is the exception, because its final vowel carries an accent. Normal: «BEH-neh», «lah-TEH» is wrong, and «LAHT-teh» is right. STEP 4: an accent mark on the last vowel shows that the stress is on the final syllable: «città» (cheet-TAH), «perché» (pehr-KEH), «università» (oo-nee-vehr-see-TAH). STEP 5: «caffè» also has an accent: the stress is on the last «è». STEP 6: the accents are part of the spelling, so write them: «perché» and «perche» are not the same word on paper.
blocos.comparacao: English stress is unpredictable: «PHOtograph», «phoTOgrapher». Italian stress is much more regular: nearly always the second-to-last syllable, unless the final vowel has an accent. The long consonants will feel strange, but they change meanings, so practice them with pairs: palla/pala, sette/sete.

erros.motivo: The accent on the last vowel is written and means the stress is there.
The accent distinguishes «perché» from other readings.
«Nono» is a different word: keep the double «n».

blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: English «How are you?» has one form. Italian has two, depending on who you are talking to. STEP 2: with a friend, a child or a person your age, say «Come stai?» (informal). STEP 3: with a stranger or an older person, say «Come sta?» (formal). The word «Lei» is the formal «you»: «E Lei?» means «And you?». STEP 4: the reply is «Sto bene, grazie» for both. For a friend, add «E tu?» (and you?); for a formal speaker, add «E Lei?». STEP 5: «bene, bene» repeated means «really fine, fine». STEP 6: «piacere» is said when you meet someone, and it also answers «Come sta?» when you meet that person for the first time.
blocos.comparacao: English adjusts the tone but not the grammar: «Hey, how are you?» and «How do you do?» are the same verb. In Italian the verb changes: «stai» for a friend and «sta» for a formal speaker. Using the wrong one is not a disaster, but «sta» is safer when you are not sure.

exemplos.pt: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
I'm fine, thank you. And you? (formal)

tabela.exemplo: Come stai?  Sto bene, grazie. E tu?
Come sta?  Sto bene, grazie. E Lei?

erros.motivo: Mixing the two forms: for health, use «Come sta?» (formal) or «Come stai?» (informal).

itens.explicacao: The accent on the last vowel marks the stress.

itens.enunciado: Which greeting do you use for a stranger?
How is the final «e» of «bene» pronounced?
itens.explicacao: Italian vowels are always pronounced and pure.

blocos.enunciado: Greet a friend and then a shop owner, using «Come stai?» and «Come sta?». Answer each one with «Sto bene, grazie».
Pronounce «palla» and «pala», «nonno» and «nono» aloud, and mark the doubled consonant.
